warmup.q: fun authorize(p: Payment): AuthCode throws CardDeclinedException when the issuer says no. A new Kotlin endpoint calls it and doesn't catch anything. What happens when a card is declined?
options: The build fails until the caller handles the exception
The exception travels up to the HTTP layer, and the customer gets a 500
Kotlin wraps the exception in a Result for the caller
warmup.why: Kotlin has no checked exceptions, so nothing in the signature or the build tells the caller that a decline is possible. The exception propagates until something catches it, usually a generic handler that turns it into a 500. In Java, a checked throws CardDeclinedException would have forced a catch. This lesson puts that information back, in the return type.

sections.h: Exceptions hide the failures your caller has to handle
sections.html:
Here is an authorization call from a checkout service, in both languages:

Java
AuthCode authorize(Payment p) throws CardDeclinedException, InsufficientFundsException;
Kotlin
fun authorize(p: Payment): AuthCode   // throws CardDeclinedException, InsufficientFundsException

In Java, checked exceptions put the failures in the signature, and the compiler makes every caller deal with them. Kotlin has none: "Kotlin treats all exceptions as unchecked by default." So the Kotlin signature only says AuthCode, and nothing tells the caller that one card in twenty comes back declined. A new endpoint forgets the try. The decline travels up to the HTTP layer, the customer gets a 500, and the on-call engineer gets paged for a card that was simply out of money.

The real problem is that two kinds of failure share one mechanism. A declined card, an expired card or an unknown currency is expected: it happens every day, and the caller must decide what to do. A null pointer, a broken invariant or a lost database connection is a bug or an environment failure, and no caller can do anything useful about it on the spot. The Kotlin team draws the same line. The design notes for kotlin.Result say: "Use nullable types or domain-specific classes to represent failures that need specific handling." The newer rich-errors proposal, KEEP-0441, says exceptions "should be used for unrecoverable cases."

So put the expected failures in the return type, as values:

Java
sealed interface AuthResult {}
record Approved(String code) implements AuthResult {}
record Refused(AuthFailure reason) implements AuthResult {}
AuthResult authorize(Payment p);
Kotlin
sealed interface AuthResult {
    data class Approved(val code: String) : AuthResult
    data class Refused(val reason: AuthFailure) : AuthResult
}
fun authorize(p: Payment): AuthResult

sealed means the compiler knows every subtype, so a when over them needs no else. That pays off when someone adds a case. Add FraudSuspected to AuthFailure and every when that doesn't handle it stops compiling: 'when' expression must be exhaustive. Add the 'is FraudSuspected' branch or an 'else' branch. Java 21's sealed interfaces and pattern switch give the same check: the switch expression does not cover all possible input values. That error is the whole point, so never write else on a sealed type. It throws the check away.

Exceptions keep their job for bugs. require, check and error() still belong wherever an invariant breaks.

try.title: Add a failure and let the compiler find the gaps
steps: Run Exhaustive.kt. Four authorizations come out as four HTTP status lines.
Uncomment FraudSuspected in AuthFailure and run it again. Read the error and note which when it points at.
Add a branch for it to httpStatus (403 is fine) and run again.
Do the same in ExhaustiveJava.java.

code.title: Exhaustive.kt
code.html: package workbench.functional.l07 /** The expected ways an authorization can fail. A closed set: the compiler knows every case. */ sealed interface AuthFailure { data class InvalidAmount(val amountMinor: Long) : AuthFailure data object CardExpired : AuthFailure data class InsufficientFunds(val shortByMinor: Long) : AuthFailure // Uncomment the next line and run again. // data class FraudSuspected(val score: Int) : AuthFailure } sealed interface AuthResult { data class Approved(val code: String) : AuthResult data class Refused(val reason: AuthFailure) : AuthResult } /** The signature now says it can fail, and how. Nothing is thrown for a decline. */ fun authorizeCard(amountMinor: Long, balanceMinor: Long, expiryYear: Int): AuthResult = when { amountMinor <= 0 -> AuthResult.Refused(AuthFailure.InvalidAmount(amountMinor)) expiryYear < 2026 -> AuthResult.Refused(AuthFailure.CardExpired) amountMinor > balanceMinor -> AuthResult.Refused(AuthFailure.InsufficientFunds(amountMinor - balanceMinor)) else -> AuthResult.Approved("A-${amountMinor % 997}") } /** The one place that knows HTTP: an exhaustive when with no else branch. */ fun httpStatus(failure: AuthFailure): Int = when (failure) { is AuthFailure.InvalidAmount -> 400 AuthFailure.CardExpired -> 402 is AuthFailure.InsufficientFunds -> 402 } fun main() { val attempts = listOf(Triple(4_250L, 10_000L, 2028), Triple(-5L, 10_000L, 2028), Triple(4_250L, 10_000L, 2024), Triple(14_250L, 10_000L, 2028)) for ((amount, balance, expiry) in attempts) { val line = when (val result = authorizeCard(amount, balance, expiry)) { is AuthResult.Approved -> "200 approved ${result.code}" is AuthResult.Refused -> "${httpStatus(result.reason)} ${result.reason}" } println(line) } }

alt.title: ExhaustiveJava.java
alt.html: package workbench.functional.l07; import java.util.List; /** The same closed set of failures with Java 21 sealed interfaces, records and an exhaustive switch. */ public class ExhaustiveJava { sealed interface AuthFailure {} record InvalidAmount(long amountMinor) implements AuthFailure {} record CardExpired() implements AuthFailure {} record InsufficientFunds(long shortByMinor) implements AuthFailure {} // Uncomment the next line and run again. // record FraudSuspected(int score) implements AuthFailure {} sealed interface AuthResult {} record Approved(String code) implements AuthResult {} record Refused(AuthFailure reason) implements AuthResult {} static AuthResult authorizeCard(long amountMinor, long balanceMinor, int expiryYear) { if (amountMinor <= 0) return new Refused(new InvalidAmount(amountMinor)); if (expiryYear < 2026) return new Refused(new CardExpired()); if (amountMinor > balanceMinor) return new Refused(new InsufficientFunds(amountMinor - balanceMinor)); return new Approved("A-" + amountMinor % 997); } /** The one place that knows HTTP: an exhaustive switch with no default branch. */ static int httpStatus(AuthFailure failure) { return switch (failure) { case InvalidAmount a -> 400; case CardExpired c -> 402; case InsufficientFunds i -> 402; }; } public static void main(String[] args) { List<long[]> attempts = List.of(new long[] {4_250, 10_000, 2028}, new long[] {-5, 10_000, 2028}, new long[] {4_250, 10_000, 2024}, new long[] {14_250, 10_000, 2028}); for (long[] a : attempts) { String line = switch (authorizeCard(a[0], a[1], (int) a[2])) { case Approved ok -> "200 approved " + ok.code(); case Refused r -> httpStatus(r.reason()) + " " + r.reason(); }; System.out.println(line); } } }

try.expect: The first run prints 200 approved A-262, 400 InvalidAmount(amountMinor=-5), 402 CardExpired and 402 InsufficientFunds(shortByMinor=4250). With the new case, Kotlin stops at httpStatus with 'when' expression must be exhaustive. Add the 'is FraudSuspected' branch or an 'else' branch. The when in main still compiles, because it only looks at AuthResult. javac reports the switch expression does not cover all possible input values at the same spot. After you add the branch, both run again.

sections.h: A result type you can write in ten lines
sections.html:
A sealed result per function gets repetitive, and chaining them is clumsy, because every step needs a when to check the step before. One generic type covers every step:

Java
sealed interface Outcome<E, A> {
    default <B> Outcome<E, B> andThen(Function<? super A, Outcome<E, B>> f) {
        return switch (this) {
            case Ok<E, A> ok -> f.apply(ok.value());
            case Err<E, A> err -> new Err<>(err.error());
        };
    }
}
record Ok<E, A>(A value) implements Outcome<E, A> {}
record Err<E, A>(E error) implements Outcome<E, A> {}
Kotlin
sealed interface Outcome<out E, out A> {
    data class Ok<A>(val value: A) : Outcome<Nothing, A>
    data class Err<E>(val error: E) : Outcome<E, Nothing>
}

inline fun <E, A, B> Outcome<E, A>.andThen(f: (A) -> Outcome<E, B>): Outcome<E, B> =
    when (this) { is Outcome.Ok -> f(value); is Outcome.Err -> this }

andThen runs the next step only if this one succeeded. An Err skips every later step and comes out at the end unchanged. Its sibling map, in the Try it, does the same for a plain function that can't fail, such as uppercase(). A payment becomes one line: validate(r).andThen(::authorise).andThen(::capture).map { it.uppercase() }.

The usual picture is a railway with two tracks, which is why this style is often called railway-oriented programming. Each step is a switch. On success the train stays on the top track. On failure it moves to the bottom track and stays there to the end, so nothing after the failure runs. The figure shows it.

Look at the variance. Outcome<out E, out A> is covariant in both parameters ("Covariance with out: producers" in the generics track), and Err is an Outcome<E, Nothing>. Nothing is a subtype of every type, so an Err<PayErr> already is an Outcome<PayErr, String>, an Outcome<PayErr, Receipt>, an Outcome<PayErr, X> for any X. That is why is Outcome.Err -> this compiles without building a new object. Java has no declaration-site variance and no Nothing, so the Java version builds a new Err at every step.

That is all an Either is at heart. Libraries add more combinators and a block syntax that makes chains read like straight-line code, which is the last section.

figure.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 640 260" role="img" aria-label="Railway diagram. A success track runs through three steps: validate, authorise, capture. From each step a branch drops to a failure track. Once on the failure track, the error travels to the end and no later step runs."><text class="t-s t-ok" x="20" y="84">success</text><text class="t-s t-bad" x="20" y="194">failure</text><line class="ln-a" x1="80" y1="80" x2="600" y2="80" marker-end="url(#arr)"/><line class="ln-bad" x1="80" y1="190" x2="600" y2="190" marker-end="url(#arr)"/><rect class="box" x="115" y="60" width="110" height="40" rx="8"/><text class="t t-code" x="170" y="85" text-anchor="middle">validate</text><rect class="box" x="275" y="60" width="110" height="40" rx="8"/><text class="t t-code" x="330" y="85" text-anchor="middle">authorise</text><rect class="box" x="435" y="60" width="110" height="40" rx="8"/><text class="t t-code" x="490" y="85" text-anchor="middle">capture</text><line class="ln-bad" x1="200" y1="100" x2="250" y2="186" marker-end="url(#arr)"/><line class="ln-bad" x1="360" y1="100" x2="410" y2="186" marker-end="url(#arr)"/><line class="ln-bad" x1="520" y1="100" x2="570" y2="186" marker-end="url(#arr)"/><text class="t-s t-bad" x="250" y="146" text-anchor="middle">Invalid</text><text class="t-s t-bad" x="412" y="146" text-anchor="middle">Declined</text><text class="t-s t-bad" x="574" y="146" text-anchor="middle">Unavailable</text><text class="t-s t-ok" x="560" y="56" text-anchor="middle">Ok(receipt)</text><text class="t-s t-bad" x="520" y="214" text-anchor="middle">Err(the first error)</text><text class="t-s t-m" x="320" y="248" text-anchor="middle">andThen runs a step only on the success track; map changes the value there</text></svg>

try.title: Ride the railway
steps: Read Outcome.kt. Each step prints its name when it runs. For each of the three requests, predict which names print and what comes out.
Run it, then run OutcomeJava.java.
In Outcome.kt, change is Outcome.Err -> this in map to is Outcome.Err -> Outcome.Err(error). Does it still compile? Why was this allowed?

code.title: Outcome.kt
code.html: package workbench.functional.l07 /** A hand-written result type: a success holding a value, or a failure holding an error. */ sealed interface Outcome<out E, out A> { data class Ok<A>(val value: A) : Outcome<Nothing, A> data class Err<E>(val error: E) : Outcome<E, Nothing> } /** Change the value on the success track; a failure passes through untouched. */ inline fun <E, A, B> Outcome<E, A>.map(f: (A) -> B): Outcome<E, B> = when (this) { is Outcome.Ok -> Outcome.Ok(f(value)); is Outcome.Err -> this } /** Run the next step that can fail, only on the success track. */ inline fun <E, A, B> Outcome<E, A>.andThen(f: (A) -> Outcome<E, B>): Outcome<E, B> = when (this) { is Outcome.Ok -> f(value); is Outcome.Err -> this } sealed interface PayErr { data class Invalid(val why: String) : PayErr data object Declined : PayErr } data class Req(val amountMinor: Long, val currency: String) fun validateReq(r: Req): Outcome<PayErr, Req> { println(" validate") return if (r.amountMinor > 0) Outcome.Ok(r) else Outcome.Err(PayErr.Invalid("amount<=0")) } fun authoriseReq(r: Req): Outcome<PayErr, String> { println(" authorise") return if (r.amountMinor < 10_000) Outcome.Ok("auth-1") else Outcome.Err(PayErr.Declined) } fun captureAuth(auth: String): Outcome<PayErr, String> { println(" capture") return Outcome.Ok("cap-of-$auth") } fun payReq(r: Req) = validateReq(r).andThen(::authoriseReq).andThen(::captureAuth).map { it.uppercase() } fun main() { for (r in listOf(Req(500, "EUR"), Req(-1, "EUR"), Req(50_000, "EUR"))) { println("$r:") println(" -> ${payReq(r)}") } }

alt.title: OutcomeJava.java
alt.html: package workbench.functional.l07; import java.util.List; import java.util.function.Function; /** The same result type in Java 21. Without declaration-site variance and Nothing, Err must be rebuilt each step. */ public class OutcomeJava { sealed interface Outcome<E, A> { default <B> Outcome<E, B> map(Function<? super A, ? extends B> f) { return switch (this) { case Ok<E, A> ok -> new Ok<>(f.apply(ok.value())); case Err<E, A> err -> new Err<>(err.error()); // a new Err with a new type }; } default <B> Outcome<E, B> andThen(Function<? super A, Outcome<E, B>> f) { return switch (this) { case Ok<E, A> ok -> f.apply(ok.value()); case Err<E, A> err -> new Err<>(err.error()); }; } } record Ok<E, A>(A value) implements Outcome<E, A> {} record Err<E, A>(E error) implements Outcome<E, A> {} sealed interface PayErr {} record Invalid(String why) implements PayErr {} record Declined() implements PayErr {} record Req(long amountMinor, String currency) {} static Outcome<PayErr, Req> validate(Req r) { System.out.println(" validate"); return r.amountMinor() > 0 ? new Ok<>(r) : new Err<>(new Invalid("amount<=0")); } static Outcome<PayErr, String> authorise(Req r) { System.out.println(" authorise"); return r.amountMinor() < 10_000 ? new Ok<>("auth-1") : new Err<>(new Declined()); } static Outcome<PayErr, String> capture(String auth) { System.out.println(" capture"); return new Ok<>("cap-of-" + auth); } static Outcome<PayErr, String> pay(Req r) { return validate(r).andThen(OutcomeJava::authorise).andThen(OutcomeJava::capture).map(String::toUpperCase); } public static void main(String[] args) { for (Req r : List.of(new Req(500, "EUR"), new Req(-1, "EUR"), new Req(50_000, "EUR"))) { System.out.println(r + ":"); System.out.println(" -> " + pay(r)); } } }

try.expect: Req(500) runs all three steps and gives Ok(value=CAP-OF-AUTH-1). Req(-1) prints only validate and gives Err(error=Invalid(why=amount<=0)). Req(50000) prints validate and authorise and gives Err(error=Declined): capture never runs. Java prints the same steps. Both versions of the Err branch compile; this works because an Outcome<E, Nothing> is already an Outcome<E, B> for every B, so there is no need to build a new object.

sections.h: kotlin.Result wraps foreign code, and swallows cancellation
sections.html:
The standard library has one result type, kotlin.Result<T>, and runCatching { } makes one. It is not an Either. It has a single type parameter, and the failure is always a Throwable. Its design notes are blunt: "The Result class is not designed to represent domain-specific error conditions." It was built mainly for the coroutine machinery: Continuation.resumeWith takes a Result.

Use it at the edge, around code that throws when you want a value back:

Java
BigDecimal rate;
try { rate = fxClient.rate("EUR", "GBP"); }
catch (Exception e) { rate = cachedRate; }
Kotlin
val rate = runCatching { fxClient.rate("EUR", "GBP") }   // a Java HTTP client that throws
    .getOrElse { cachedRate }

Two traps come with it. The first is that runCatching catches every Throwable. That includes OutOfMemoryError and StackOverflowError, and inside a coroutine it includes CancellationException, the exception that carries a cancel ("Cancellation and timeouts" in the coroutines track). The Try it cancels a coroutine while it waits inside runCatching. The cancel turns into a failed Result, the coroutine runs on until its next suspension point, and the line that charges the card runs. An issue asking kotlinx.coroutines for a runCatching that rethrows CancellationException (#1814) has been open since February 2020. Until something ships, rethrow it yourself, as the lab asks:

Java
// Java equivalent: never swallow the interrupt that carries a cancel
try { return issuer.authorize(req); }
catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); throw new CancellationException(); }
Kotlin
runCatching { issuer.authorize(req) }
    .onFailure { if (it is CancellationException) throw it }   // a cancel keeps travelling

The second trap is that map doesn't catch. runCatching { "12".toLong() }.map { error("boom") } throws IllegalStateException: boom straight out of map. Only mapCatching turns it into Failure(java.lang.IllegalStateException: boom). The library pairs recover and recoverCatching the same way. If a chain should be safe end to end, every step that can throw needs the Catching variant.

So Result answers one question: did this throwing call work? It can't say which payment failure happened, so keep it out of your domain signatures. fun capture(id: String): Result<Receipt> tells the caller less than the sealed type from the first section.

try.title: Cancel a payment inside runCatching
steps: Read part 1 of RunCatchingTrap.kt. The coroutine is cancelled after 50 ms, while it waits inside runCatching. Predict: does charging card anyway print, and what is in the ledger?
Run it and compare part 1 with part 2.
Read part 3 and predict which line throws.
Run RunCatchingTrapJava.java, which makes the same mistake with a thread and catch (Exception e).

code.title: RunCatchingTrap.kt
code.html: package workbench.functional.l07 import kotlinx.coroutines.cancelAndJoin import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.isActive import kotlinx.coroutines.launch import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking import kotlin.coroutines.cancellation.CancellationException fun main() = runBlocking<Unit> { println("1. runCatching around a suspend call, cancelled after 50 ms:") val ledger = mutableListOf<String>() val swallowing = launch { val r = runCatching { delay(1_000); "auth-1" } println(" runCatching returned: isFailure=${r.isFailure} ex=${r.exceptionOrNull()?.javaClass?.simpleName}") println(" isActive after swallow = $isActive") ledger += "charged card" println(" charging card anyway (code with no suspension point keeps running)") try { delay(1) } catch (e: CancellationException) { println(" next suspension point throws: ${e.javaClass.simpleName}") throw e } } delay(50) swallowing.cancelAndJoin() println(" ledger: $ledger") println("2. the same, with CancellationException rethrown:") val ledger2 = mutableListOf<String>() val rethrowing = launch { val r = runCatching { delay(1_000); "auth-1" }.onFailure { if (it is CancellationException) throw it } ledger2 += "charged card ($r)" } delay(50) rethrowing.cancelAndJoin() println(" cancelled=${rethrowing.isCancelled}, ledger: $ledger2") println("3. map rethrows, mapCatching captures:") val parsed = runCatching { "12".toLong() } println(" mapCatching: ${parsed.mapCatching { error("boom") }}") try { parsed.map { error("boom") } } catch (e: IllegalStateException) { println(" map threw: IllegalStateException: ${e.message}") } }

alt.title: RunCatchingTrapJava.java
alt.html: package workbench.functional.l07; import java.util.List; import java.util.concurrent.CopyOnWriteArrayList; /** * Java equivalent of RunCatchingTrap.kt: a catch-everything block around a blocking call swallows the * interrupt, the thread's cancel signal, and the code after it charges the card anyway. */ public class RunCatchingTrapJava { public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { System.out.println("1. catch (Exception e) around sleep, interrupted after 50 ms:"); List<String> ledger = new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>(); Thread swallowing = new Thread(() -> { try { Thread.sleep(1_000); // the issuer call } catch (Exception e) { System.out.println(" caught " + e.getClass().getSimpleName() + ", carrying on"); } ledger.add("charged card"); }); swallowing.start(); Thread.sleep(50); swallowing.interrupt(); swallowing.join(); System.out.println(" ledger: " + ledger); System.out.println("2. the same, with the interrupt restored and the work stopped:"); List<String> ledger2 = new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>(); Thread stopping = new Thread(() -> { try { Thread.sleep(1_000); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); // keep the signal return; // and stop } ledger2.add("charged card"); }); stopping.start(); Thread.sleep(50); stopping.interrupt(); stopping.join(); System.out.println(" ledger: " + ledger2); } }

try.expect: Part 1 prints runCatching returned: isFailure=true ex=JobCancellationException, isActive after swallow = false, then charging card anyway, and only the next delay throws. The ledger holds charged card: work ran after the cancel. Part 2 rethrows, so the job ends cancelled=true with an empty ledger. In part 3, mapCatching returns Failure(java.lang.IllegalStateException: boom) and map throws. Java's thread catches InterruptedException, carries on and charges the card; restoring the flag and returning fixes it.

sections.h: Arrow's Either: fail fast, or collect every error
sections.html:
Arrow is a functional programming library for Kotlin, and the lab uses arrow-core 2.3.0. Its Either<E, A> is the Outcome from earlier, Left(error) or Right(value), plus an either { } block that replaces the chains of andThen:

Java
// Java equivalent: the hand-written Outcome from the last section, chained with andThen
Outcome<PaymentError, Receipt> pay(ValidPayment p) {
    return gateway.authorize(p).andThen(auth -> {
        int score = gateway.riskScore(auth);
        if (score >= 80) return new Err<>(new FraudSuspected(score));
        return gateway.capture(auth).map(capture -> new Receipt(auth, capture));
    });
}
Kotlin
fun pay(p: ValidPayment): Either<PaymentError, Receipt> = either {
    val auth = gateway.authorize(p).bind()                   // a Left ends the block here
    val score = gateway.riskScore(auth)
    ensure(score < 80) { PaymentError.FraudSuspected(score) }
    val capture = gateway.capture(auth).bind()
    Receipt(auth, capture)
}

Inside either { }, .bind() unwraps a Right. On a Left it stops the block, and that Left becomes the result. ensure(condition) { error } stops the block when the condition is false. The code reads top to bottom like the happy path, and it is fail-fast: the first failure wins, and nothing after it runs.

Fail-fast is right for a pipeline, where each step needs the one before. It is wrong for a form. A client that sends a negative amount and an unknown currency should hear about both at once, not one per round trip. zipOrAccumulate runs independent checks, collects every failure into a NonEmptyList, and calls its last lambda only if all of them passed:

Java
// Java equivalent: run every check and collect the errors by hand
Validated<Amount> validate(long a, String c) {
    List<FormError> errors = new ArrayList<>();
    if (a <= 0) errors.add(new InvalidAmount(a));
    if (!CURRENCIES.contains(c)) errors.add(new UnsupportedCurrency(c));
    return errors.isEmpty() ? new Valid<>(new Amount(a, c)) : new Invalid<>(List.copyOf(errors));
}
Kotlin
fun validate(a: Long, c: String): Either<NonEmptyList<FormError>, Amount> = either {
    zipOrAccumulate({ validAmount(a) }, { validCurrency(c) }) { amount, currency -> Amount(amount, currency) }
}
// validate(-5, "XYZ") is Either.Left([InvalidAmount(amountMinor=-5), UnsupportedCurrency(code=XYZ)])

validAmount and validCurrency are functions with a Raise<FormError> receiver that call ensure. The same input through a plain either { Amount(validAmount(-5), validCurrency("XYZ")) } gives only Either.Left(InvalidAmount(amountMinor=-5)).

For foreign code, Either.catch { } is the safer cousin of runCatching. It turns an ordinary exception into a Left, but it rethrows CancellationException and fatal errors such as OutOfMemoryError.

You may have read that Kotlin is getting error unions, fun load(): User | NotFound. That is a real proposal (KEEP-0441, with the detailed design in KEEP-0462), but it is not in Kotlin 2.4.21: the compiler rejects error class NotFound with Syntax error: Expecting a top level declaration. Today the picker is short. Use a nullable type when absence needs no reason. Use a sealed type for a few outcomes of one function. Use Either when many steps chain or errors must accumulate. Keep Result for throwing foreign code, and exceptions for bugs.

try.title: Fail fast, then collect everything
steps: Read EitherDemo.kt. Predict what failFast(-5, "XYZ") and accumulate(-5, "XYZ") print.
Run it.
Change the accumulate call to accumulate(4_250, "XYZ"). Predict the result, then run it.
Run EitherDemoJava.java and compare how much code the Java version needs per rule.

code.title: EitherDemo.kt
code.html: package workbench.functional.l07 import arrow.core.Either import arrow.core.NonEmptyList import arrow.core.raise.Raise import arrow.core.raise.either import arrow.core.raise.ensure import arrow.core.raise.zipOrAccumulate import kotlin.coroutines.cancellation.CancellationException sealed interface FormError { data class InvalidAmount(val amountMinor: Long) : FormError data class UnsupportedCurrency(val code: String) : FormError } data class Amount(val minor: Long, val currency: String) fun Raise<FormError>.validAmount(a: Long): Long { ensure(a > 0) { FormError.InvalidAmount(a) } return a } fun Raise<FormError>.validCurrency(c: String): String { ensure(c in setOf("EUR", "USD", "GBP")) { FormError.UnsupportedCurrency(c) } return c } /** Stops at the first failure: the second check never runs. */ fun failFast(a: Long, c: String): Either<FormError, Amount> = either { Amount(validAmount(a), validCurrency(c)) } /** Runs every check and collects every failure. */ fun accumulate(a: Long, c: String): Either<NonEmptyList<FormError>, Amount> = either { zipOrAccumulate({ validAmount(a) }, { validCurrency(c) }) { amount, currency -> Amount(amount, currency) } } fun main() { println("fail fast: ${failFast(-5, "XYZ")}") println("accumulate: ${accumulate(-5, "XYZ")}") println("all good: ${accumulate(4_250, "EUR")}") println("Either.catch around foreign code:") println(" ${Either.catch { "12x".toLong() }.mapLeft { it::class.simpleName }}") try { Either.catch { throw CancellationException("job cancelled") } } catch (e: CancellationException) { println(" CancellationException rethrown, not captured") } }

alt.title: EitherDemoJava.java
alt.html: package workbench.functional.l07; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; import java.util.Set; /** Java equivalent: the JDK has no Either. A small sealed result and a list of errors do both jobs by hand. */ public class EitherDemoJava { sealed interface FormError {} record InvalidAmount(long amountMinor) implements FormError {} record UnsupportedCurrency(String code) implements FormError {} record Amount(long minor, String currency) {} sealed interface Validated<A> {} record Valid<A>(A value) implements Validated<A> {} record Invalid<A>(List<FormError> errors) implements Validated<A> {} static final Set<String> CURRENCIES = Set.of("EUR", "USD", "GBP"); /** Stops at the first failure: the second check never runs. */ static Validated<Amount> failFast(long a, String c) { if (a <= 0) return new Invalid<>(List.of(new InvalidAmount(a))); if (!CURRENCIES.contains(c)) return new Invalid<>(List.of(new UnsupportedCurrency(c))); return new Valid<>(new Amount(a, c)); } /** Runs every check and collects every failure. */ static Validated<Amount> accumulate(long a, String c) { List<FormError> errors = new ArrayList<>(); if (a <= 0) errors.add(new InvalidAmount(a)); if (!CURRENCIES.contains(c)) errors.add(new UnsupportedCurrency(c)); return errors.isEmpty() ? new Valid<>(new Amount(a, c)) : new Invalid<>(List.copyOf(errors)); } public static void main(String[] args) { System.out.println("fail fast: " + failFast(-5, "XYZ")); System.out.println("accumulate: " + accumulate(-5, "XYZ")); System.out.println("all good: " + accumulate(4_250, "EUR")); } }

try.expect: fail fast: Either.Left(InvalidAmount(amountMinor=-5)): the currency check never ran. accumulate: Either.Left([InvalidAmount(amountMinor=-5), UnsupportedCurrency(code=XYZ)]). With a good amount, only Either.Left([UnsupportedCurrency(code=XYZ)]) remains: still a list, now with one element. Either.catch turns "12x".toLong() into Either.Left(NumberFormatException) and lets the CancellationException through. Java prints the same results with a hand-built list.

refs.title: Working with typed errors, Arrow docs source

analogy: An exception is a fire alarm: it stops everything and sends people running to the exits, whatever they were doing. That is right for a fire. It is wrong for a declined card, which is more like a returned letter: it comes back in the normal post, in an envelope marked "address unknown", and whoever opens the mail decides what to do. Errors as values turn expected failures into returned letters, so they travel the same route as the good news and the reader can't miss them. The analogy breaks at the edges: a letter can be thrown away unread, and so can an Either. By default, Kotlin 2.4.21 doesn't warn about an ignored return value.
world: A payments service has failures at three levels, and this lesson gives each one a home. Request validation in a Quarkus REST endpoint should accumulate, so the client fixes the whole form at once: Either<NonEmptyList<ValidationError>, PayCommand>, turned into one 400 response. The business pipeline (authorize, risk check, capture, ledger) is fail-fast, an either { } block over Either<PaymentError, Receipt>. At the outbound edge, the adapter for the card network turns the few infrastructure failures that have a business meaning into values (a SocketTimeoutException becomes ProviderUnavailable, which a Temporal workflow can retry) and lets everything else propagate to the global handler and the alerting. A Kafka consumer that settles batches should never wrap its loop in plain runCatching: on shutdown it would keep processing after the cancel.
mistake: The most common mistake is wrapping a coroutine's work in runCatching "so one failure doesn't kill the loop". It reads like a safe try/catch, which is why people reach for it. But it catches every Throwable, including the CancellationException that a shutdown, a timeout or a cancelled parent sends. The coroutine stays cancelled, yet the code after runCatching keeps running until it hits a suspension point, and a loop can log a long list of "failed" items that never failed. The fix is to let cancellation through: rethrow CancellationException in onFailure, use a wrapper like the lab's runCatchingCancellable, use Arrow's Either.catch, or best of all catch only the exception types you expect from that call.

compare.title: A fail-fast payment pipeline: Java sealed result vs Kotlin either { }

java.title: Payments.java
java.html: sealed interface Outcome<E, A> { /* map and andThen as in section 2 */ } record Ok<E, A>(A value) implements Outcome<E, A> {} record Err<E, A>(E error) implements Outcome<E, A> {} Outcome<PaymentError, Receipt> pay(ValidPayment p) { return gateway.authorize(p).andThen(auth -> { // 1. authorize int score = gateway.riskScore(auth); // 2. risk check if (score >= FRAUD_THRESHOLD) return new Err<>(new FraudSuspected(score)); return gateway.capture(auth) // 3. capture .map(capture -> new Receipt(auth, capture)); }); }

kotlin.title: Payments.kt
kotlin.html: fun pay(p: ValidPayment, gateway: Gateway): Either<PaymentError, Receipt> = either { val auth = gateway.authorize(p).bind() // 1. authorize val score = gateway.riskScore(auth) // 2. risk check ensure(score < FRAUD_THRESHOLD) { PaymentError.FraudSuspected(score) } val capture = gateway.capture(auth).bind() // 3. capture Receipt(auth, capture) }

compare.note: Both are the same railway: the first Err or Left ends the pipeline and comes back unchanged, and the sealed error type keeps every when or switch over it exhaustive. The differences are in how it reads and what the library brings. Java nests a lambda per step, so a five-step pipeline drifts to the right, and every Err has to be rebuilt because Java has no Nothing and no declaration-site variance. Kotlin's either { } keeps the steps flat: bind() and ensure stop the block with the error, so the code reads like the happy path. Arrow also brings what the hand-written version lacks: zipOrAccumulate and mapOrAccumulate for collecting errors, Either.catch that respects cancellation, and mapLeft and recover for translating errors between layers.

worked.title: Layer a payment endpoint: validate everything, then fail fast

steps.say: A payment request arrives at a REST endpoint. 1. Validate it at the edge and collect every problem, because the client should fix the whole form in one round trip. The lab's validate returns Either<NonEmptyList<PaymentError>, ValidPayment>.
steps.code: val checked: Either<NonEmptyList<PaymentError>, ValidPayment> = validate(request) // PaymentRequest(-5, "XYZ", "1", "r") gives Left([InvalidAmount(amountMinor=-5), UnsupportedCurrency(code=XYZ), InvalidCardNumber(last4=1)])

alt.html: Validated<ValidPayment> checked = validate(request); // every rule runs; the errors are collected if (checked instanceof Invalid<ValidPayment> invalid) return badRequest(invalid.errors());

steps.say: 1. Run the business steps fail-fast, and give the two kinds of error one type so the endpoint can return either. mapLeft translates the error side and leaves a Right alone.
steps.code: sealed interface ApiError { data class Invalid(val errors: NonEmptyList<PaymentError>) : ApiError data class Failed(val error: PaymentError) : ApiError } fun handle(request: PaymentRequest, gateway: Gateway): Either<ApiError, Receipt> = either { val valid = validate(request).mapLeft(ApiError::Invalid).bind() // every form error at once pay(valid, gateway).mapLeft(ApiError::Failed).bind() // the first business failure }

alt.html: sealed interface ApiError {} record InvalidRequest(List<PaymentError> errors) implements ApiError {} record Failed(PaymentError error) implements ApiError {} Outcome<ApiError, Receipt> handle(PaymentRequest request, Gateway gateway) { return switch (validate(request)) { case Invalid<ValidPayment> invalid -> new Err<>(new InvalidRequest(invalid.errors())); // every form error case Valid<ValidPayment> valid -> switch (pay(valid.value(), gateway)) { // the first business failure case Ok<PaymentError, Receipt> ok -> new Ok<>(ok.value()); case Err<PaymentError, Receipt> err -> new Err<>(new Failed(err.error())); }; }; }

steps.say: 1. At the outbound edge, turn the one infrastructure failure that has a business meaning into a value, and let everything else propagate. A timeout becomes ProviderUnavailable, which a workflow can retry; an IllegalStateException is a bug and must stay an exception.
steps.code: fun Http.charge(body: String): Either<PaymentError, String> = Either.catch { post(body) } // rethrows CancellationException and fatal errors .mapLeft { e -> if (e is SocketTimeoutException) PaymentError.ProviderUnavailable else throw e }

alt.html: Outcome<PaymentError, String> charge(Http http, String body) throws IOException { try { return new Ok<>(http.post(body)); } catch (SocketTimeoutException e) { return new Err<>(new ProviderUnavailable()); // the one failure with a business meaning } // other exceptions propagate: a bug stays a bug }

steps.say: 1. Map errors to HTTP in exactly one place, with an exhaustive when and no else. When someone adds a PaymentError case next year, this function stops compiling until they decide its status code.
steps.code: fun httpStatus(error: ApiError): Int = when (error) { is ApiError.Invalid -> 400 is ApiError.Failed -> when (error.error) { PaymentError.CardDeclined, is PaymentError.FraudSuspected -> 402 PaymentError.ProviderUnavailable -> 503 is PaymentError.InvalidAmount, is PaymentError.UnsupportedCurrency, is PaymentError.InvalidCardNumber, is PaymentError.ReferenceTooLong -> 400 } }

alt.html: int httpStatus(ApiError error) { return switch (error) { case InvalidRequest i -> 400; case Failed f -> switch (f.error()) { case CardDeclined d -> 402; case FraudSuspected s -> 402; case ProviderUnavailable u -> 503; case InvalidAmount a -> 400; case UnsupportedCurrency c -> 400; case InvalidCardNumber n -> 400; case ReferenceTooLong r -> 400; }; }; }

lab.title: Validate everything, fail fast, and keep cancellation
steps: Run the tests. Ten of twelve fail. The two that pass check runCatchingCancellable with a value and an ordinary exception, where plain runCatching already works. Model.kt holds the types and needs no changes.
In Validation.kt, write checkCardNumber and checkReference in the style of the two rules above them.
Write validate as either { zipOrAccumulate(...) { ... } }, with the four checks in the order the KDoc gives.
In Pipeline.kt, write pay as one either { } block: bind() each gateway call that returns an Either, and ensure the fraud score.
In SafeCatching.kt, make runCatchingCancellable rethrow CancellationException. The cancellation test runs on the virtual time of kotlinx-coroutines-test, so it finishes at once.
Run the tests until all twelve pass.
hints: zipOrAccumulate takes up to nine lambdas and then a final lambda that receives their results. Inside each lambda you can call the check... functions directly, because the lambdas run in a Raise context.
In pay, read the score into a val first, then ensure(score < FRAUD_THRESHOLD) { PaymentError.FraudSuspected(score) }.

Import CancellationException from kotlin.coroutines.cancellation. Catch it before the general Throwable clause and rethrow it, or use runCatching { block() }.onFailure { if (it is CancellationException) throw it }.
If either or zipOrAccumulate won't resolve, add import arrow.core.raise.either and import arrow.core.raise.zipOrAccumulate.

drill.title: A railway from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write Outcome<E, A> with its two cases, map and andThen, with the variance that lets an error pass through unchanged. Then chain validate, authorise and capture with it. Check: does your Err branch need to build a new object?

answer.html: sealed interface Outcome<out E, out A> { data class Ok<A>(val value: A) : Outcome<Nothing, A> data class Err<E>(val error: E) : Outcome<E, Nothing> } inline fun <E, A, B> Outcome<E, A>.map(f: (A) -> B): Outcome<E, B> = when (this) { is Outcome.Ok -> Outcome.Ok(f(value)); is Outcome.Err -> this } // Err<E> is an Outcome<E, B> inline fun <E, A, B> Outcome<E, A>.andThen(f: (A) -> Outcome<E, B>): Outcome<E, B> = when (this) { is Outcome.Ok -> f(value); is Outcome.Err -> this } fun pay(r: Req) = validate(r).andThen(::authorise).andThen(::capture)

alt.html: sealed interface Outcome<E, A> { default <B> Outcome<E, B> map(Function<? super A, ? extends B> f) { return switch (this) { case Ok<E, A> ok -> new Ok<>(f.apply(ok.value())); case Err<E, A> err -> new Err<>(err.error()); // Java must rebuild the Err }; } default <B> Outcome<E, B> andThen(Function<? super A, Outcome<E, B>> f) { return switch (this) { case Ok<E, A> ok -> f.apply(ok.value()); case Err<E, A> err -> new Err<>(err.error()); }; } } record Ok<E, A>(A value) implements Outcome<E, A> {} record Err<E, A>(E error) implements Outcome<E, A> {} Outcome<PayErr, String> pay(Req r) { return validate(r).andThen(this::authorise).andThen(this::capture); }

recap: Expected failures, such as a decline or an unknown currency, belong in the return type as values. Bugs and broken infrastructure stay exceptions.
A sealed result with an exhaustive when and no else makes the compiler list every case you forgot to handle.
A two-case result with map and andThen is a railway: each step runs only on the success track. out variance and Nothing let an error pass through unchanged.
kotlin.Result wraps throwing foreign code. runCatching catches every Throwable, CancellationException included, and map doesn't catch: use mapCatching.
Arrow's either { } with bind and ensure is fail-fast; zipOrAccumulate runs every check and collects the errors in a NonEmptyList.
Error unions like User | NotFound are a proposal (KEEP-0441, KEEP-0462). Kotlin 2.4.21 rejects the syntax.

explain.prompt: A teammate proposes fun capture(paymentId: String): Result<Receipt> for the new capture service, "because Result is Kotlin's built-in way to return errors". Explain why it's a poor fit, and what you would use instead.
explain.answer: Result has one type parameter, and its failure side is always a Throwable, so the signature says "this can fail somehow" and nothing about how. The caller can't tell a decline from an expired authorization from a provider outage without inspecting exception classes, and the compiler won't check that every case is handled. The Kotlin team's own design notes say Result isn't meant for domain errors. It also comes from runCatching, which catches CancellationException and fatal errors unless you're careful. I'd model the expected failures as a sealed CaptureError (AuthorizationExpired, AlreadyCaptured, ProviderUnavailable, ...) and return Either<CaptureError, Receipt>, or a sealed result type if we don't want Arrow. Then a when over the error is exhaustive, adding a case breaks the build where it must be handled, and real bugs stay exceptions for the global handler.

deeper.html:
Three parts of Arrow are worth knowing once either { } feels natural.

Raise without Either. The lab's checks are functions with a Raise<PaymentError> receiver: they don't return an Either, they raise inside whatever block calls them. Kotlin 2.4.0 made context parameters Stable, and Arrow 2.3.0 ships matching versions of ensure, raise and bind in the arrow.core.raise.context package, so the same check can be written as context(_: Raise<PaymentError>) fun checkCurrency(code: String): String. With Kotlin 2.4.21 that compiles without any compiler flag. Arrow's own docs still show the extension-receiver style and describe context parameters as a future option, so expect both styles in code you read.

Collections and the experimental DSL. mapOrAccumulate validates every element of a list and collects the failures: running it over the amounts [10, -1, 20, -2] gives Either.Left([InvalidAmount(amountMinor=-1), InvalidAmount(amountMinor=-2)]). There is also an accumulate { ensureOrAccumulate(...) } block that reads like a list of checks. In Arrow 2.3.0 it is still marked @ExperimentalRaiseAccumulateApi, so you opt in with @OptIn(ExperimentalRaiseAccumulateApi::class); zipOrAccumulate is the stable choice.

Translating errors between layers. mapLeft changes the error value and leaves a Right alone, as in the worked example. recover is more general: inside it you can run any computation that may itself raise, for example falling back to a second acquirer when the first returns ProviderUnavailable. Use mapLeft to rename errors at a boundary, and recover to handle them.
